terms.comment: To read a text out to listeners: a letter, a law, a list, one’s own poems; clārē, out loud. Under the Empire authors read their new works to invited audiences, the recitātiōnēs of Pliny’s letters (Lewis & Short).

evidence: Plin. Ep. 9.36.3: clārē et intentē … legō

terms.gloss: read aloud to a class, read with explanations
evidence: Suet. Gram. 16: Vergilium et aliōs poētās (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The teacher’s reading, to show how a text should be read and to explain it; Lewis & Short: post-Augustan. The reading is praelēctiō (see lecture).

phrases.latin: Cedo sānē mihi. — At clārē recitātō. — Tacē, dum pellegō.
phrases.english: Give it here, then. — But read it out loud. — Quiet, while I read it through.

phrases.latin: ōrātiōnem Graecam Latīnamve clārē et intentē nōn tam vōcis causā quam stomachī legō
phrases.english: I read a speech, Greek or Latin, aloud and with effort, not so much for my voice’s sake as for my digestion’s

phrases.latin: Lege (legite) clārē (lentius, celerius, clārius, flexā vōce).
phrases.english: Read aloud (slower, faster, louder, with expression).

sources: Lewis & Short: recito · Lewis & Short: clare · Lewis & Short: praelego
